Nāstika Darśanas
------------------------------------------
Indian philosophical systems—known as Darśanas—have been broadly grouped under two categories: the आस्तिक and the nāsitka.
All those systems which accept the authority of the वेदस् are called ‘āstika’ whereas those that do not, are branded as ‘nāstika’. The Cārvāka, the Jaina and the Bauddha systems are classified under the latter.

nāstika
(‘atheist’)
------------------------------------------
A नास्तिक is one who says ‘It does not exist!’ (na = not, asti = exist). He does not believe in the existence of God, the सोउल्, after-life, हेअवेन् and hell—in fact all that cannot be experienced by the five sense-organs.
See CĀRVĀKA-DARŚANA.

Nāsik
------------------------------------------
Visiting places of पिल्ग्रिमगे as a part of religious duty imposed by the scriptures of one’s faith or for getting spiritual inspiration is a universal phenomenon found in all the great religions of the world.
Out of the several important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे listed by the पुराणस् and the निबन्धस् (digests) नासिक् is also one. It is a district headquarters in Maha-rashtra and is 10 kms. (6.2 miles) from the Nasik Road railway station.
नासिक्">Godāvarī at NāsikIt was probably known as Nāsikya or Navaśikhara in the olden days. The first name might have been derived because of the cutting of the nose (= nāsikā) and ears of शूर्पणखा by लक्ष्मण at this place. Alternatively, since there are nine peaks (= nava-शिखर) of small mountains nearby, it might have been christened ‘Navaśikhara’.
It is sometimes called ‘Paścimakāśī’ and the गोदावरी river, the banks on which it is situated, named ‘Gaṅgā’ also.
Nāsik is one of the four holy places where the great bathing festivals and religious fairs known as ‘Kumbhamelā’ are held. It takes place when the planet बृहस्पति or गुरु (Jupiter) enters the zodiacal sign Siṁha (Leo), once in twelve years. A bath in the गोदावरी during this period—technically called ‘Puṣkara’—is considered as extremely auspicious.
The गोदावरी river takes its birth in the Brahmagiri hill near Tryambakeśvar, about 32 kms. (20 miles) from नासिक्. The temple of Tryambakeśvar contains one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस्.
Pañcavaṭī, where राम, सीता and लक्ष्मण camped during their banishment from अयोध्या and from where सीता was abducted by रावण is to the north of नासिक् town. This spot was known as Padmanagara in the कृतयुग, Trikaṇṭaka in the त्रेतायुग, जनस्थान in the द्वापरयुग and Nāsika in the कलियुग.
Nāsik once abounded in temples most of which were destroyed by Aurangazeb (A.

-1707). Among these were the temples of नारायण, Umāmaheśvara, राम, Kapāleśvara and महालक्ष्मी. Most of the surviving temples were built during the rule of the Peṣvas of Maharashtra.
The temple of Sundaranārāyaṇa is situated in the Āditwārpeṭ, facing east. There are three images—the image of नारायण in black stone, 91.5 cms. (3 ft.) in height is at the centre, flanked by two smaller images of Śrīdevī and Bhūdevī—in the shrine. The image of नारायण is so situated that on the 20th or 21st March every year, the sun’s rays at sunrise fall on his feet.
The Kālārām temple (temple of राम with the image in black stone) is another well-known structure frequented by the pilgrims. It is built on a जगती (platform) 87 metres (285 ft.) by 32 metres (105 ft.). It was constructed in A.

. There are two more temples, of नारायण and Bhadrakālī, which too are well-known.
Another temple at Mālegāse built by the king Nārū Śaṅkar, has a nice bell cast in Portugal.
Sītāgumpha (or guhā) in पञ्चवटी the cave where सीता is said to have been kept and protected, is another important spot visited by the pilgrims. It contains the images of राम, सीता, लक्ष्मण and a लिङ्ग of Pañcaratna महादेव.
There are a few, very old and tall Banyan trees that are believed to have sprung up from the original trees (that were there when राम arrived).
There are numerous bathing places and pools (known as kuṇḍas) between गोवर्धन (10 kms. or 6 miles to the west of नासिक्) and Tapovana (2.5 kms. or 1½ miles to the south-west of नासिक्). The Rāmakuṇḍa near the left bank of the गोदावरी where it turns towards the south, is considered the holiest of these kuṇḍas.
Near नासिक् there are more than 20 Buddhist caves known as Pāṇḍuleṇā-guhās where the bhikkus used to live during the rainy season.
Many archaeological finds have been discovered near नासिक्, belonging to the prehistoric eras, as also stone inscriptions of later period (200 B. C. to A.

Nāsadīyasūkta
(‘the सूक्त [beginning with the word] “nāsad” ’)
------------------------------------------
How exactly the च्रेअतिओन् of this world came about, this world of myriads of mysteries and insoluble riddles, has been too knotty a problem to be satisfactorily solved by the puny human intellect, which itself is a product of the whole process! The effect cannot discover its cause, even as we cannot see our own back.
However, we can see our back provided we use two mirrors, one at the back and the other in our front, properly adjusted. Similarly, if we can judiciously use the knowledge of the Śruti (the वेदस्) to back up our intellect and be guided by the sayings and doings of the ṛṣis, persons of intuitive or superconscious (spiritual) experience, we can succeed in getting some glimpses of the secrets of च्रेअतिओन् that will ultimately help us in reaching the final goal of our life. Study of selected parts of the वेदस् like the Nāsadīyasūkta, is a great aid in this endeavour of ours to attain perfection.
The Nāsadīyasūkta is a part of the Ṛgveda (10.129.1-7). प्रजापति Parameṣṭhī is said to be the ṛṣi (sage) to whom it was revealed. Paramātmā (God, the Creator, called ‘Bhāvavṛttam’ by सायण, the commentator) is the devatā or the deity. Triṣṭubh is the metre in which it is composed.
This is a wonderful and highly poetic hymn that describes what existed before च्रेअतिओन् and how च्रेअतिओन् came about.
The Sūkta begins with an account of what existed before च्रेअतिओन्. Since हिन्दुइस्म् posits a cyclic theory of च्रेअतिओन् —sṛṣṭi (creation or evolution), sthiti (sustenance) and प्रलय or लय (destruction or involution), taking place eternally in that order—this description applies to all cycles. That (or He) alone—the ब्रह्मन् of the उपनिषद्स् or God of religion—existed, the One without a second, breathing (living) by himself though without breath. There was deep blinding darkness everywhere. However, that One, ब्रह्मन्, through intense tapas—self-reflection or profound thinking—became (through his own greatness or power) transformed into this world. Actually, this desire to create arose in him due to the ‘seed’ in his मिन्द्, the unmanifested karmas of the beings carried over from the previous cycle. The ṛṣis or sages possessing transcendental or intuitive wisdom, had discovered this secret.
As ब्रह्मन् willed the evolution of this world, the inanimate (various objects) and the animate (the jīvas or the living beings) got manifested, the latter being superior to the former.
This evolution went on continuously, producing not only the पञ्चभूतस् (the five primordial elements) but also the देवस् (gods who exercise control over these).
However, this process—how the One became the many—remains a mystery even to these देवस्, since they too came afterwards.
This ब्रह्मन्, the Supreme Being, not only created this world (out of his free will) but is also sustaining it.
If he does not do this, who else can?
The whole secret of च्रेअतिओन् is known only to him. If he cannot, who else can?
This is the gist of the whole Sūkta.
In this hymn we find a very advanced theory of च्रेअतिओन् which is developed later in the उपनिषद्स् also (vide Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.7; Chāndogya Upaniṣad

and so on).
It is interesting and even puzzling to note that the sage to whom this Sūkta was revealed, has used quite a few mutually contradictory words and phrases. For instance, he says: There was then neither what is (sat) nor what is not (asat)... There was no death (mṛtyu) and hence nothing immortal (amṛta). There was no night (rātri) nor day (ahan).
The only explanation that can be offered for the use of apparently contradictory terms is that in the beginning there was only the One (tat) and there was no second person or object when and when only comparative statements are possible.
